extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, agency lawyers, and regulatory policy practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for when an agency may invoke the APA 'good cause' exception to issue an interim final rule (IFR), and how courts should review and constrain IFRs (including sunset, finalization, and the role of notice-and-comment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show IFR likely objectively superior to the regulatory status quo
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must show that the IFR is likely to lead to objectively superior outcomes compared to the regulatory status quo; courts should stay an IFR if the agency fails to show it likely would be objectively better than the status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld proposes a 'likely superior' standard similar in nature to the likelihood-of-success standard for preliminary injunctions. Example: the Attorney General's SORNA retroactivity IFR was problematic because it relied on mere possibility rather than evidence that retroactivity would reduce sexual offenses. Courts should not uphold IFRs justified only by speculative or merely possible benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain evidence and identify persuasive considerations when technical uncertainty exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when courts give deference on technical facts, an agency must acknowledge factual uncertainties and 'identify the considerations it found persuasive' and 'explain the evidence which is available' and the 'rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Rural Cellular Ass'n v. FCC and State Farm: agencies receive extreme deference on technical matters, but that does not permit mere recitation of 'substantial uncertainty.' The agency should offer the evidence available and a reasoned explanation linking facts to choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value judgments are insufficient to justify invoking good cause for an IFR
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's reliance on subjective value judgments (political, moral, or purely evaluative preferences) to justify an IFR is insufficient; courts should stay such IFRs and await notice-and-comment FFRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld explains that value-judgment justifications are inherently political and risk undoing prior-administration rules without notice; example: HHS contraception 'moral exemptions' where comparative benefits depended on contested values. Student scholarship also argues constitutional and moral harms are invalid reasons for invoking good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFRs should not be used to effectuate political preferences or to avoid notice-and-comment scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may not properly invoke good cause to adopt IFRs primarily to satisfy White House political goals or to energize an administration's political base; notice-and-comment is needed for such political matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld notes that political pressure can short-circuit deliberation and hide objective tradeoffs; using IFRs for politically-driven changes undermines transparency and the public input function of notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reasoned decisionmaking; courts must not simply accept agency conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although courts defer to agency expertise, they must ensure agency action is supported by 'reasoned decisionmaking' and not accept conclusions simply because they reflect the agency's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Tripoli Rocketry Ass'n and Allentown Mack Sales: deference does not excuse lack of reasoned explanation. Agency conclusions must be supported by a record and rationale sufficient to survive arbitrary-and-capricious review.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFRs should be finalized promptly; problem of permanent IFRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should act to finalize an FFR as soon as practicable; many IFRs remain in effect indefinitely, which undermines the notice-and-comment regime and may produce suboptimal, less-deliberative rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asimow's ACUS study: agencies did not finalize 42–53% of IFRs in examples; excluding airworthiness directives, about 27% of IFRs remained three years later. Seidenfeld argues allowing IFRs to remain permanent thwarts congressional oversight and incentives embedded in the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFRs should include a sunset provision tailored to the rule's complexity and information needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should require IFRs to include sunset provisions, but not a universal fixed period; the sunset length should consider the regulatory issue's nature, technicality, and the burden of collecting and analyzing information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency—best positioned to know necessary time—should propose the sunset period as part of its good-cause justification and explain why it would be unreasonable to finalize earlier. This balances immediate rule benefits with the need for later reconsideration in light of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must justify the proposed sunset period when invoking good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the APA-required justification for invoking good cause, the IFR should explain why it would be unreasonable for the agency to have to finalize the IFR prior to the sunset date and propose an appropriate sunset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld suggests agencies might justify a sunset by pointing to historical time it took to adopt similar rules after publishing a NOPR or by reference to the anticipated burden of collecting relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may treat agency extensions of sunsets as final agency action only in rare, newly-arising emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may amend or extend an IFR sunset only if a genuine emergency—unknown at the time of issuance and universally recognized as paramount—requires it; courts would likely reverse improper extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld acknowledges rare catastrophic events (e.g., pandemic) might justify extension but expects courts to scrutinize and likely reverse extensions that were foreseeable when the IFR was issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider agency inaction on finalizing an IFR (letting it sunset) as reviewable final agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency takes no action and allows an IFR to sunset, that inaction should be treated as reviewable agency action; courts should consider letting an IFR sunset, adopting the IFR as final, or amending it all as final actions subject to judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld proposes that treating inaction as reviewable avoids agencies factoring defense costs into their final decision and prevents agencies from gaming the system by leaving IFRs in place without meaningful justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must meaningfully consider and respond to comments generated by an IFR
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing an IFR does not absolve an agency of the obligation to digest comments and consider whether a superior FFR should replace the IFR; failure to do so often indicates improper use of IFRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld explains reasons agencies fail to finalize (political trigger satisfied, staff resource allocation, desire to avoid scrutiny). Notice-and-comment serves both to improve substantive decisionmaking (hard look) and to provide political signaling to Congress and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal sunset period; avoid mechanical rule — allow agency-specific tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: There should not be a single standard sunset period for all IFRs because rules vary in complexity and information demands; courts should evaluate the reasonableness of the sunset based on rule-specific factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld rejects a universal rule while still advocating mandatory sunset provisions; acknowledges some statutes already impose statutory deadlines for finalizing equivalents to IFRs (e.g., temporary tax regs, emergency endangered species listings).

rubrics_metrics.name: IFRs addressing widely agreed-upon objective dangers may be justified if predictions are supportable
rubrics_metrics.description: If an IFR is issued because the agency discovered dangers in the status quo that reasonable observers would agree are harms to be avoided, then the agency's factual predictions (if supportable) can justify issuing an IFR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld distinguishes these cases from those based on value judgments: when there is an objective consensus about danger, the question is whether the agency's predictions about the rule's efficacy are supportable by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts can require procedural measures necessary to make APA meaningful (consistent with Vermont Yankee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Vermont Yankee limits courts from adding procedures beyond the APA, courts may require measures (like sunset provisions) necessary to ensure agency invocation of the good cause exception actually satisfies APA criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld argues requiring sunset provisions can be justified as necessary for the APA to function meaningfully; cites case law where courts have required agencies to reveal studies relied upon despite Vermont Yankee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware agency resource-allocation rationales that evade notice-and-comment obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's claim that devoting resources to finalizing an IFR is inefficient is not a sufficient reason to avoid notice-and-comment; the APA envisions resource commitment when an agency decides to adopt a final legislative rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seidenfeld recognizes resource constraints and rare tradeoffs (e.g., catastrophic events) but stresses that generally resource-saving should not be used as a pretext to forgo deliberation and public participation.
